title: Nexus
description: Full-stack project management application with authentication, task tracking, Kanban board, and analytics. Built with Next.js App Router, Server Actions, and Prisma.

caseStudy.projectOverview: Nexus began as an exercise in shipping a complete product from a single idea: a task manager that consumed an external REST API. The question that kept pulling me back was what would change if I took ownership of the entire stack instead of stopping at the frontend. That question became the reason to migrate the application incrementally to a server-first architecture using Server Components, Server Actions, and Prisma ORM, making the project as much a migration exercise as a product. Nexus is intentionally developed in cycles: I pause it to explore other products and return with new ideas, architectural improvements, and lessons learned elsewhere. Rather than targeting a fixed final state, it acts as a long-term environment for evolving my full-stack, product, and SaaS practices.
whyThisStack: Next.js App Router enables Server Components and Server Actions, removing the need for a separate API layer and reducing client-side state management
Prisma ORM provides type-safe database access that integrates cleanly with TypeScript and keeps the schema and application queries aligned
Auth.js v5 manages credentials, Google OAuth, sessions, and route protection within the Next.js architecture
Zod validates data at application boundaries, while a centralised ActionResult type gives Server Actions a consistent success and error contract
Nodemailer supports password recovery through standard SMTP without tying the application to a transactional email provider
keyFeatures: Google OAuth and email/password authentication with password recovery and rate limiting
Database queries scoped by user to keep account data isolated
Task management with filtering, pagination, tagging, priorities, and status tracking
Kanban board with drag and drop, organised by project
Analytics dashboard with priority distribution and task status charts, built with Recharts
Reusable Server Actions with a centralised ActionResult type and Zod validation
challengesTradeoffs: Migrating incrementally from React Query and Axios to Server Actions without breaking existing product behaviour
Designing a scalable actions architecture by splitting monolithic files into co-located, independently tested modules
Balancing server-side simplicity with interactive client behaviour by defining the 'use client' boundary carefully
Maintaining architectural consistency in a long-running project that evolves through separate development cycles
whatILearned: Incremental migrations are easier to validate and recover from than rewriting an entire application at once
Server-first architecture removes a lot of client-side complexity once data ownership and mutation boundaries are clearly defined
Authentication is more than a login screen: data isolation, rate limiting, password recovery, and route protection all need to work together
A consistent action result contract improves both developer experience and the quality of user-facing error feedback
A long-running project needs explicit architectural conventions so it can evolve without accumulating disconnected patterns
nextSteps: Explore SaaS foundations through multi-user workspaces and billing
Add end-to-end test coverage with Playwright

title: Redirect Lab
description: Full-stack link management platform with custom short URLs, access tracking, cross-tab synchronisation, accessible interactions, infinite scrolling, and CSV export through Cloudflare R2.

caseStudy.projectOverview: Redirect Lab started as a postgraduate assignment: a URL shortener called Brev.ly, built to explore full-stack development end to end. When I looked at it again for my portfolio, the assignment was done, but the project itself wasn't finished. I rebuilt it as an independent React client and Fastify API, each deployable on its own, with automated accessibility checks, stronger testing practices, and a cost-conscious cloud architecture designed to run for little or no cost.
whyThisStack: React and TanStack Query provide a focused client architecture with explicit server-state caching, mutation feedback, and paginated data loading
Fastify and Drizzle ORM create a lightweight, type-safe API and persistence layer aligned with the TypeScript domain model
Zod provides predictable validation at application boundaries and prevents invalid data from moving between the client and API
Vitest, Testing Library, and axe-core support behavioural and accessibility testing without relying on external testing services
Vercel, Railway, Neon, and Cloudflare R2 allow the client, API, database, and generated files to be deployed independently using practical free or low-cost tiers
keyFeatures: Custom short URL creation with validation and duplicate prevention
Access tracking with cross-tab count synchronisation through BroadcastChannel
Paginated link loading with infinite scrolling and IntersectionObserver
CSV export stored on Cloudflare R2 and delivered through a public URL
Accessible forms, dialogs, controls, keyboard interactions, and focus states with automated axe checks
Responsive dark and light themes
challengesTradeoffs: Separating the original monorepo while preserving its history and allowing the client and API to evolve independently
Replacing the original AWS delivery setup with lower-cost services without sacrificing deployment reliability
Keeping access counts synchronised across browser tabs without adding WebSockets or an external real-time service
Balancing useful product features with a focused scope by postponing authentication and advanced analytics
Improving the original architecture without losing the simplicity expected from a focused link management product
whatILearned: A course assignment can become a maintainable product when its original constraints are reassessed instead of carried forward automatically
Separating the frontend and API improves deployment independence but requires clearer contracts and validation between applications
Reliable server-state handling depends on planned cache invalidation, mutation feedback, and loading states
Accessibility is more effective when treated as part of interaction design and continuously checked through automated tests
Operating cost is an architectural constraint that can guide simpler and more appropriate infrastructure decisions
nextSteps: Explore an access analytics dashboard with clicks grouped by period
Consider QR code generation and PNG download as future product extensions

title: Auth Starter
description: Reusable Next.js authentication foundation created to remove repetitive setup from new projects. Split into a clean template and a public documentation and demo site.

caseStudy.projectOverview: I kept rebuilding the same authentication setup at the start of every new project: users, sessions, protected routes, password recovery. Auth Starter exists to remove that repetition. Authentication, database integration, OAuth, and password recovery often require the same decisions before product work can even begin. The project separates those responsibilities into two repositories: a clean template intended to be copied and adapted, and a public website responsible for documentation, presentation, and the future live demo.
whyThisStack: Next.js App Router provides server-rendered routes, Route Handlers, and a clear boundary between public and protected application areas
Better Auth offers a stable modern API for credentials, OAuth, sessions, and password recovery
Prisma and PostgreSQL provide type-safe relational persistence that can be reused across different products
Zod provides predictable validation at application boundaries, keeping configuration and inputs explicit
Nodemailer provides provider-independent SMTP delivery for password recovery emails
Separating the site and template repositories prevents generated projects from inheriting portfolio and documentation code
keyFeatures: Reusable email and password authentication flow
Optional Google OAuth configuration
Server-validated protected routes
PostgreSQL persistence through Prisma
Password recovery flow with SMTP email delivery through Nodemailer
Per-route rate limiting persisted in Postgres, safe for stateless serverless functions
Automated unit and integration test suite with CI
Separate public site and clean template repositories
Public project site with an adaptive visual identity and favicon for light and dark browser themes
challengesTradeoffs: Defining what belongs to the reusable template and what belongs only to the public demonstration site
Choosing Better Auth stable instead of building the starter on the still-beta Auth.js v5 API
Balancing a complete authentication foundation with a template that remains small and easy to understand
Planning for future automation without prematurely introducing the complexity of a CLI
whatILearned: Reusable foundations require stricter separation of responsibilities than product-specific applications
Documentation should follow a validated implementation instead of defining behaviour too early
A template repository and an installable package solve different problems
Version stability is an important architectural consideration for reusable developer tooling
nextSteps: Evaluate adding Google OAuth and end-to-end browser test coverage
Disconnect unused infrastructure (Railway) and verify production environment variables
Evaluate a future create-nextjs-auth-starter CLI after using the template in real projects
